v: Next year, Calgary wants fifteen percent more in property tax. So we asked one simple question. Is that about growth, or about spending?
Calgary has grown fast. About one point six million people now, roughly a fifth more than in twenty twenty-one. If growth is the reason, the numbers should line up.
So we added it up. Population growth plus inflation comes to about sixteen percent by twenty thirty. The tax plan adds about forty-four. Almost three times as much.

So where does the rest go? The biggest single piece is not police, and not transit. It is water. Pipes and treatment plants are more than forty percent of the new spending, and that comes on your water bill, on top of your taxes.
But here is the part nobody talks about. That fifteen percent is not the same for everyone.

Picture two neighbours. One owns a semi-detached house. The other owns a condo down the street. Condo values have been falling, while houses have barely moved. So the house could pay about eighteen percent more, and the condo about eight. Same city. Same budget. Very different bills.
And the growth itself? Half of it landed in just five wards, mostly on the city's edges. Those wards have about a third fewer transit stops per person, and far fewer City recreation sites.

So, growth or spending? Our answer is: both, but mostly spending. Growth and inflation explain part of the increase. The rest is the City doing more per person, on water, on transit, and on services Council asked for. Whether that is worth it, is Calgary's call.
And Council can still change the number. Ten percent instead of fifteen would mean about one hundred twenty-eight million dollars less to spend next year.
Council debates the budget from November twenty-third. The full study, with every number, is at calgary insight dot c a. So tell us. Is fifteen percent fair? Drop your answer in the comments.
